Page29 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version 3.4 PROXIMITY TO EXISTING INFRASTRUCTURE The proposed T-RICH hub site is perfect for use as a CO intermodal hub due to 1) being surrounded by 2 numerous existing industrial facilities and 2) the existence of several suitable modes of transportation nearby with relatively little work necessary to tie the site directly into them. The primary infrastructure required for T-RICH, with its planned export of CO on ocean-going marine vessels, is a ship berth. There 2 is an existing deep-water berth at the site ready to accept a large CO vessel with minor modifications to 2 receive the hub’s processed and liquified CO and load it for transport to the permanent sequestration or 2 EOR site in the northern Gulf region. See Section 4.5.12 for a detailed discussion on this berth. The next type of infrastructure needed to make T-RICH a true intermodal hub is an incoming rail line. There is a main rail line owned by U.S. rail operator CSX within one mile of the site, with an existing spur owned by Port Tampa Bay running down Pendola Point peninsula which serves the terminal adjacent to T-RICH. An extension of this rail line can be installed onto the proposed hub site, as confirmed by Port Tampa Bay engineers. CSX operates a rail network of over 20,000 miles serving 23 states. Figure 3.10 shows this existing rail network in blue with the T-RICH site depicted as a red dot. Existing rail lines run very close by, or even directly adjacent to, several of the large power plants shown in the central part of the state in Figure 3.8. For example, a rail line currently runs to the entrance of Duke’s Hines Energy Complex which is the single largest point source of CO emissions identified in this study (4.2 mtpa of CO 2 2 emissions). Existing rail lines also run to within approximately 500 feet of the generators at both the CD McIntosh Jr. Power Plant and the Osprey Energy Center, both in Lakeland, FL. This existing rail network can be leveraged to transport large quantities of CO captured at plants across the state to T-RICH even 2 without significant investments in pipelines, and the associated long lead times involved with pipeline permitting and construction. An incoming pipeline to T-RICH is, however, considered ultimately necessary to make the overall CO 2 transportation system, of which T-RICH is a critical part, cost effective. There are currently no CO pipelines 2 in the region which the hub can make use of, and new, relatively short pipelines to transmit CO captured 2 by the region’s major stranded emitters to T-RICH will incur high capital costs.
